marker_every: kila, the distributive determiner ("kila Jumatatu" = every Monday).
marker_from: The opening half of a range, closed by hadi/mpaka.
marker_future: future relative-time pattern is "baada ya <unit> {0}" -- literally "after",
the same preposition that introduces a plain succession.
marker_last: relative-type--1 per unit, and the relative pronoun agrees with the noun
class of the unit it follows: "mwaka uliopita" and "mwezi uliopita" take the
class 3/4 form, while "wiki iliyopita" and every weekday -- "Jumatatu
iliyopita" -- take the class 9/10 form.  zilizopita is the class 9/10 plural,
the shape CLDR counts with above one ("wiki {0} zilizopita").
All three ship together because a marker slot is matched by surface: which
one is grammatical is decided by the noun the writer already chose, and a
writer who chose it correctly must be read.

marker_past: Unicode CLDR 47, cldr-json cldr-dates-full/main/sw/dateFields.json.  The past
relative-time pattern is the unit noun, the count, and the same agreeing
relative pronoun the bare last/this/next phrases use -- "miaka {0} iliyopita"
= N years ago, "mwaka {0} uliopita" = one year ago, "wiki {0} zilizopita".
So "ago" is not a separate word in Swahili: the marker that says "last week"
says "N weeks ago" as well, and both surfaces sets are the same three.
marker_since: tangu is the past-anchored half of the from/since pair: it opens a stretch
reaching from a point already gone up to now.  kutoka, the forward "from",
stays in marker_from where it opens a closed range against hadi/mpaka.
marker_this: relative-type-0: "mwaka huu" / "mwezi huu" for class 3/4, "wiki hii" / "saa
hii" / "dakika hii" and "<weekday> hii" for class 9/10.
marker_until: Reaching a point in time: the closing half of the "kutoka X hadi Y" range.

unit1_second: Class 9/10 nouns do not change for number, so the singular is the same word.
unit_day: {0} iliyopita" / "siku {0} zilizopita" -- class 9/10, invariant for number.
unit_hour: saa is a DURATION here and only a duration.  The same word names the hour of
the day, and that reading is deliberately not shipped: Swahili's traditional
clock counts the hours from sunrise, so "saa tatu" is 09:00 to one writer and
03:00 to another, and nothing in the phrase says which.  See
test/nl_corpus_sw/test_sw_refusals.py for the pinned refusal, and lang.json
for the clock grammar that admits the digital literal only.
unit_minute: {0} iliyopita" / "dakika {0} zilizopita" -- class 9/10, invariant for number.
unit_month: {0} uliopita" in the singular and "miezi {0} iliyopita" in the plural: mwezi
is class 3/4, so unlike the N-class units it DOES change shape for number,
and the plural miezi is what a count above one stands beside.
unit_second: second field counts with one surface in both plural categories ("Sekunde {0}
iliyopita", "Sekunde {0} zilizopita"): sekunde is class 9/10 and invariant,
so the noun carries no count and the count lives in the numeral alone.
